title: The Sightline Vote
primary_metric: sightline safety score per dollar of construction cost

options.A: Recommend The Squared Corner -- buy the two corner-lot slivers and reconstruct the intersection at a full 90-degree angle
options.B: Recommend The Offset Bypass -- build the new connector lane parallel to the existing platted lot line, at the intersection's existing skew angle, with no land purchase

sources.claim: Minimum interior intersection angle for an at-grade public roadway intersection
sources.title: Highway Design Manual, Chapter 400 -- Intersections at Grade, Topic 403.3 "Angle of Intersection"
sources.note: Reproduced on up.codes, a code-reference site, from Caltrans HDM Chapter 400; the primary Caltrans PDF did not extract cleanly for direct fetch (attempted, recorded in RESEARCH_LOG.md), so this is a well-attributed republication rather than the primary document itself. Exact quote: 'the interior angle should be designed as close to 90 degrees as is practical, but should not be less than 75 degrees.' Used in this case as the real state minimum standard both contractors claim to clear.

sources.claim: A real, quantitative relationship exists between intersection angle and crash safety; agencies should reconsider critical-minimum-angle design policy accordingly
sources.value: qualitative finding, no specific formula reproduced
sources.org: Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), Turner-Fairbank Highway Research Center

sources.note: Primary federal research source; confirmed via the report's own HTML index/abstract page (the full PDF did not extract cleanly for direct fetch, recorded in RESEARCH_LOG.md). deliverables.text: A labeled plan-view site diagram of the current intersection and of each redesign option, marking a fixed point, a line segment (curb edge, both endpoints labeled), a ray (the driver's sightline), and the vertex where the two road centerlines meet.

For the current skewed intersection, find all four angles from the stated skew angle, classify each as acute or obtuse, show adjacent pairs are supplementary, and show the vertical pairs are congruent.
For The Squared Corner, confirm the four right angles the redesign creates, and show the ADA curb ramp splits one right angle into two complementary angles, finding both.

For The Offset Bypass, show the new connector lane is parallel to the platted lot line, and use the lot line's given angle to find the resulting angle where the connector meets Kellner Avenue, naming the angle-pair relationship used.
A sightline-safety-score-per-dollar comparison for each option, from the angle values in D2-D4 and the construction costs in Appendix C; state the winner and margin.

balance.argument_a: The Squared Corner achieves the maximum possible sightline safety score -- sin(90 deg) = 1.0, the best any redesign can score -- clearing the real 75-degree state minimum [S1] with the largest possible margin, not just barely meeting it. Its total cost ($485,880: $400,000 shared base reconstruction + $80,000 land for the two corner slivers + 280 ft of new curb-and-gutter at $21/ft) is only 18.6% more than Option B's, because the shared base reconstruction dominates both totals -- the land purchase is a real but comparatively modest addition on top of work the city has to do either way.
balance.argument_b: The Offset Bypass wins the case's actual graded metric -- safety score per dollar -- by 14.56%, using real geometry (the connector lane's 75-degree angle to Kellner Avenue is derived directly from the platted lot line via the parallel-lines/transversal relationship, not assumed) and a real sourced construction rate [S3]. Its 75-degree sightline angle exactly meets the real state minimum standard [S1] -- code-compliant, not a near-miss -- while needing no land acquisition and no title work, and its total cost ($409,660) is lower than Option A's in absolute dollars despite needing more linear feet of new curb-and-gutter, because it avoids the $80,000 land line entirely.
balance.margin_basis: Sightline safety score (sin of the acute intersection angle, Appendix B) divided by each option's total construction cost (Appendix C: shared base reconstruction + Option A's land acquisition + each option's own curb-and-gutter footage at the sourced per-foot rate), computed in cases/the-sightline-vote/sensitivity_model.py.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Shared base intersection reconstruction cost (signal loop, drainage tie-in, ADA ramps, base course paving), identical for both options
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public cost estimate exists for this specific intersection's exact scope. Comparable real small-municipality projects found during research bracket this figure: a minor signage/striping/curb-radii-only safety fix can run as little as $42,000 (Waller County, TX mobility-bond project list), while a full state-highway-scale realignment can run into the millions (e.g. a $9.37M realignment, and a separate $4M PennDOT skew-correction project); this case's scope (drainage, signal, and pavement work at a local two-lane/four-lane intersection) sits well above the minor fix and well below a state-highway project.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Identical for both options, so it does not change which option wins -- only how close the two totals are. Flexed +/-50% in Tier 2 probe 5; the margin is sensitive to this value even though the winner is not (see sensitivity_note).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Land acquisition cost, two corner-lot slivers (Option A only)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public appraisal exists for these specific, not-yet-acquired slivers. Right-of-way acquisition research indicates corner parcels near a signalized or high-traffic intersection carry a real, documented acquisition premium over a mid-block parcel of the same size; this case prices two narrow slivers (not full lots) at a modest small-town value consistent with that premium.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Load-bearing on Option A's total cost and on the margin. Flexed +/-50% in Tier 2 probe 5.

sensitivity_note: Unlike a case where the graded metric is pure geometry, here MA1 and MA2 both enter the total-cost denominator directly, so the MARGIN is genuinely sensitive to both -- flexing either +/-50% (holding the other at its stated value) never flips the winner (Option B wins at every tested combination) but does move the margin outside the SPEC section 2 20% band at the extremes (as low as ~5% and as high as ~32%). This is disclosed here and in FACILITATOR.md rather than hidden: the WINNER is stable under both assumptions; the exact SIZE of B's win is not, and a Hero who treats 14.56% as a fixed fact rather than a modeled estimate has missed the point of Appendix D.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public cost record exists for this specific, fictional intersection's exact reconstruction scope. $400,000 is a documented good-faith estimate bracketed between two real comparable public projects found in research (a $42,000 signage/striping-only fix and multi-million-dollar state-highway realignments) -- the closest public analogues, not a direct citation for this quantity. Flexing it +/-50% pushes the margin to 8.7%-31.7% (never flips the winner).

No public appraisal exists for these specific, not-yet-acquired corner-lot slivers. $80,000 is a documented good-faith estimate informed by right-of-way acquisition literature showing a real corner-parcel premium near intersections, applied to two narrow slivers (not full lots) at small-town scale -- not a direct citation for this quantity. Flexing it +/-50% pushes the margin to 5.1%-24.0% (never flips the winner).
